newsitem.title: CUBA: Pope to visit Cuba in 1998, church officials say.
newsitem.headline: Pope to visit Cuba in 1998, church officials say.

text.p: Pope John Paul will make his planned trip to communist-ruled Cuba in January 1998, Cuban Cardinal Jaime Ortega said on Friday.

Ortega made the announcement in a statement issued just before an evening Mass at Havana cathedral. The Mass was presided over by the visiting president of Italy's Roman Catholic bishops' conference, Cardinal Camilo Ruini.

Ruini announced the timing in his homily at the service. The news was greeted with prolonged applause from the congregation, although some of the faithful may have been disappointed they will have to wait a year to see the pontiff.

It was agreed the pope would make a trip to Cuba, the only Spanish-speaking Latin American country he has not visited, at an historic first meeting between the pontiff and President Fidel Castro at the Vatican last November.
A date had not been announced, although the Vatican initially said the trip would take place during 1997.

Ruini gave no reason for the delay, but Ortega explained in his statement it would have been too hasty to organise a papal trip for the first half of 1997, adding the hot Cuban summer was not suitable for a visit.
The pontiff was due to visit Brazil in October, and it had been agreed his trip to Cuba should not be tacked onto another visit, but should be a journey exclusively to the island, Ortega added.

"The Holy Father wants to visit our country and he would have liked to do so before the end of 1997, but the Christmas festival and other festivals around this time oblige him to postpone his visit to Cuba until January 1998," Ortega said.

The Cuban cardinal said it was initially thought the trip could take place in late November or early December this year. But the Pope conveyed through Ruini that this delay of a few days was because of his busy annual programme, Ortega added.
The 76-year-old Pope already has several other foreign trips planned in 1997. Since surgery to remove his appendix last year, he has been told by doctors to reduce his workload.

The meeting between Castro and the Pope, and the announcement that the Pope would visit Cuba marked a clear improvement in recent months in ties between Cuba's communist authorities and the Roman Catholic church.
State media said Ruini met Castro on Friday afternoon, but did not give details of their talks.
In his homily, Ruini reiterated what has become a familiar message from the Catholic church, a call for reconciliation among Cubans.

Ruini repeatedly stressed Cubans should follow a path of tolerance and reconciliation. Diversity was a social good, he said, calling for appreciation of "social, cultural and religious differences between individuals and countries."

Shortly after Castro took power in 1959, Cuba was declared a socialist state. Some 350 Catholic schools were nationalised and more than 100 priests expelled. Freedom of worship and religious instruction are limited to church premises.

Although authorities have sought since the late 1980s to show more tolerance toward the island's Christian churches, tensions with the Roman Catholic church persisted, partly over periodic criticism of the political system by the Catholic bishops.

Such tensions have eased recently -- although church officials continue to ask for the church to play a wider public role in Cuba. Vatican Foreign Minister Jean Louis Tauran referred to the need to let the church expand its role when he visited Havana last October, but refrained from making any public comment on the political system.
